description: We are an always improving team looking to build a cool project!
summary:
Agricultural General Intelligence (AGI) is a tool to make it easy for farmers to integrate various NASA datasets as well as data from external sources, allowing them to better plan crop rotations. It integrates data from 17 sources and makes this available through an intuitive frontend. Farmers can select their fields, then view the available data and crop history. AGI also features an algorithm that factors in the available data for the farmer’s fields and computes optimal crop rotations for the next five years. In recognition of the fact that farmers have to balance their priorities, this crop rotation offers three strategies: Optimize for soil health, optimize for income, and a balanced approach.

Please note that the scoring system for this algorithm is based on what we’ve learned about soil health during the course of this project, and uses example data where real data is not available. A production version of AGI would require empirical testing and validation of this algorithm to ensure it produces viable results.
details:
The intended benefit of AGI is to take as much work as possible out of the process of planning crop rotations, allowing farmers to spend more of their time focusing on their goals and how to achieve them. The net effect of this is that the farmers will be able to increase yields and income over time, improving their economic situation and also contributing to a reduction in food scarcity.

From a technical standpoint, our application is deployed as three separate services. All of the NASA data retrieval functionality occurs in the Python data backend. We chose Python for this task as it has many libraries available that help make the process of retrieving the data easier and more straightforward than hand-writing the requests from scratch.

All application logic lives in the Java / Spring Boot backend. This includes the crop rotation algorithm, the AI chat and tool functionality, and some additional data retrieval from non-NASA sources which there are no Python libraries available. This application is the single point of contact for the frontend, and the frontend does not contact the Python backend or any other data source directly. We chose Java as we are already familiar with it, and Spring Boot has robust AI tool support through Spring AI. This made it very straightforward to create the application backend which allows us more time to focus on the algorithm and other unique features.

The frontend is written in React with TypeScript, built with Vite. We chose React because the app is a guided four-step flow (location, fields, crops, results) that holds a lot of state at once: the selected fields, the crop history loading in the background, the farmer's confirmed answers and the assistant's conversation. React's components let us build each step separately while sharing that state between them. TypeScript gives us typed models of the backend's API responses, so a change on the Java side shows up as an error in the editor rather than a bug in the browser. This is the same idea as the OpenAPI specification, and it helps keep AI models on track for the same reason. For the map we used MapLibre GL, an open-source map library that draws thousands of field outlines smoothly, and lets the farmer click or drag to select fields without any paid map service. The season playback draws satellite pixels directly onto a canvas, so each 30 m square is shown exactly as measured instead of being smoothed into an image. The frontend never calls the data service directly: every request goes through the Java backend. We also kept it usable for anyone, with plain language, large touch targets, keyboard selection on the map and screen reader support, and checked every screen at desktop and phone sizes.

We used AI to assist us in various aspects of this project. For example:

- Research into the available datasets and sources

- Research of the various aspects that affect soil health

- Code generation and documentation

You may notice that our applications include unit / integration testing and OpenAPI specification. This would normally be out of scope for a hackathon submission, but in our case, it is easier to keep AI models on track between multiple developers if the models are able to access structured data on the intended API surface and functionality as well as run unit tests to validate it's own work. The upfront time spent on this is paid for as the project grows in scope.
